stimulus.text: From President Woodrow Wilson’s Fourteen Points address to Congress, January 8, 1918: “What we demand in this war, therefore, is nothing peculiar to ourselves. It is that the world be made fit and safe to live in; and particularly that it be made safe for every peace-loving nation which, like our own, wishes to live its own life, determine its own institutions, be assured of justice and fair dealing by the other peoples of the world as against force and selfish aggression.”

source: original; stimulus verbatim public-domain text, Woodrow Wilson, Fourteen Points address to Congress, January 8, 1918, public domain.
stem: In the passage, Wilson justifies American participation in the war primarily as a fight to...

options.text: make the world safe for nations to choose their governments and live free of aggression.
win new colonies and markets for the United States in Europe and Asia.
options.misconception: Wilson speaks of nations living their own lives, not of winning colonies or markets for America.

options.text: punish Germany by taking its territory and forcing it to pay for the war.
options.misconception: Punishing Germany is absent from the passage; Wilson demands safety and justice, not revenge.

options.text: build a large American empire overseas like those of Britain and France.
options.misconception: Wilson’s words oppose empire; he promises self-determination, not an American empire.

rationales.A: Wilson’s own phrases give the answer: nations should “determine its own institutions” and live free “as against force and selfish aggression.” The war, in his telling, defends self-government rather than winning spoils.
rationales.B: Wilson speaks of nations living their own lives. He says nothing about winning colonies or markets for America.
rationales.C: Punishing Germany is absent from the passage. Wilson demands safety and justice, not revenge.
rationales.D: Wilson’s words oppose empire. He promises self-determination, not an American empire overseas.
rationales.general:
1. Underline Wilson’s verbs. Nations should live their own lives and determine their own institutions.
2. Underline his enemy. The danger is “force and selfish aggression,” not a rival’s colonies or trade.
3. Test each option against those words. Only one option talks about self-government and freedom from aggression.
4. Notice what Wilson leaves out. There is no talk of territory, punishment, or empire.
Remember: when a leader states a war aim, match the option to his own words before you match it to what happened later.
